passage.title: Reading Part 2 - Test 02
passage.text:
Coffee has become one of the most popular beverages in the world, but its journey from the highlands of Ethiopia to cafes worldwide is a fascinating story. Legend has it that coffee was discovered by an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi in the 9th century. He noticed that his goats became unusually energetic after eating berries from a particular tree. Curious about this phenomenon, Kaldi tried the berries himself and experienced a similar boost in energy.

The cultivation and trade of coffee began in the Arabian Peninsula. By the 15th century, coffee was being grown in Yemen, and by the 16th century, it had spread to Persia, Egypt, Syria, and Turkey. Coffee was not only enjoyed in homes but also in public coffee houses, which became centers for social activity and communication. These establishments were sometimes called "Schools of the Wise" because they were places where people gathered to exchange ideas and discuss current events. This tradition of coffeehouses as intellectual meeting places continues in many parts of the world today.

Coffee arrived in Europe in the 17th century and quickly gained popularity, though not without controversy. Some religious leaders called it the "bitter invention of Satan" and tried to have it banned. However, Pope Clement VIII, after tasting coffee, declared it acceptable for Christians to drink. The first European coffeehouse opened in Venice in 1645, and by the end of the century, coffeehouses had spread across the continent. They became important venues for business transactions and social interaction.

Today, coffee is grown in more than 70 countries, primarily in the tropical regions of the Americas, Africa, and Asia. The industry provides livelihoods for millions of people worldwide. Modern coffee culture has evolved significantly, with specialty coffee shops offering a wide variety of brewing methods and flavors. Despite these changes, coffee remains what it has always been: a beverage that brings people together and facilitates conversation and connection.
